summary.verdict: The page picks four goals with a clear selection story and names one real risk from a named farmer, which some winners never do. It falls short of the winners where judges check each goal: no target numbers, stakeholders without names or changes, almost no numbers about your own work, and nothing on other SDGs. Several claims also contradict ReLeaf's Results, Plants, Entrepreneurship, Education and Human Practices pages.
strengths: A two-step method for choosing SDGs, and an honest reason for dropping Climate Action.
The dependence risk raised by Ms. Chen, written openly in its own section.
Measured before and after survey results for SDG 4, which few winners have for their own work.
A concrete cross-subsidy and rental plan for small farmers that matches the Entrepreneurship page.
Problems written about real groups: families who eat what they grow, small farms that cannot take risks.
priorities: Fix the claims that contradict other pages: the Arabidopsis "proven" claim, "entirely natural" protectants, the SDG list, 5 against 6 years, three schools against four visits, organic against natural.

Rewrite the abstract sheet. Its lead and two bold messages are what a judge remembers, and now they say how you started choosing goals and that your product "doesn’t promote longevity". Lead with the four goals and one line each, and give the risk its reason.

Give every goal the same parts: target number, a named stakeholder with what changed, long-term impact, and one risk. Human Practices already holds the material (Gilbert Nkpeniyeng, Ms. Chen's change, Mr. Chen's damage warning, the LINE platform, the seed exchange).
Add a section on other SDGs: who loses and which goal is hurt (power, farm work, older farmers).
Put your own numbers in the text, such as survey gains, price and containment, and use "could" for anything not yet tested in the field.
Cut the general opening lines in Overview, Negatives and Long-term impact, and correct the 2030 deadline.

ballot.question: Did the team incorporate feedback from relevant Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) stakeholders into their work?
ballot.note: USE-GH and Ms. Chen appear, but USE-GH's leader is unnamed and neither entry says what ReLeaf changed, although Human Practices records both changes.

ballot.question: Did the team address potential long-term social, environmental and economic impacts of their work (in the context of the SDG(s) they have chosen)?
ballot.note: Social impact rests on the education website; environmental and economic impact appear only as hopes inside the SDG 2 and SDG 15 solutions.

ballot.question: How well has the team considered the positive and/or negative interactions of their work in relation to other SDGs?
ballot.note: One risk (plant dependence) inside your own goals; no other SDG is named as gaining or losing from the project.

ballot.question: Has the team documented their work against their chosen SDG(s) so that other teams can build upon their work?
ballot.note: The education website is reusable, but there is no link, no list of contents, and nothing for the other three goals or earlier iGEM teams.

ballot.question: Has the team's work measurably and significantly addressed one or more SDGs?
ballot.note: Pre and post survey gains exist for SDG 4 only, and they sit in a chart; SDG 2, 10 and 15 have no measured number, and the SDG 2 claim overstates the plant data.

releaf: 2. Why we chose the SDGs that we did
3. Our SDGs: SDG 2, 4, 10, 15, each with Problem and Solution
winners: Short intro naming the project and the 3 to 5 goals claimed
One section per goal: why this goal (one context statistic), target(s), how the project contributes, stakeholder input and what changed, long-term impact
Negative interactions, per goal or in one closing section
Links to evidence pages or subpages
skeleton.gap: Your goal sections have only Problem and Solution. Winners also put the target, the stakeholder and what changed, the long-term impact and the risk inside each goal, so judges find every ballot answer in the same place each time.

extras: "That is what sustainability is to GEMS-Taiwan": the team name has no hyphen on Human Practices and Entrepreneurship. Write "GEMS Taiwan", or use "ReLeaf" as the rest of this page does.
"all of which are targets that we actively considered": SDG 2, 4, 10 and 15 are goals. Targets are the numbered parts inside a goal, such as 2.4. Write "all of which are goals".
"Early on into the project": this mixes two phrases. Write "Early in the project".
"intense adverse effects to stress": the preposition is wrong. Write "strong harm from stress".
"explain about synthetic biology to the public": "explain" needs no "about". Write "explain synthetic biology to the public".
"make the resulting crops to be unhealthy": "make" takes no "to be". Write "make the resulting crops unhealthy".
"once taken off of our protectants": drop "of". Write "once taken off our protectants".
"small scale farmers": add a hyphen before a noun. Write "small-scale farmers".
The contents list says "2. Why these SDGs", but the heading says "Why we chose the SDGs that we did". Use the same short name in both places.
Abstract sheet, On this page: "what sustainability is to GEMS-Taiwan" repeats the hyphen slip. Write "GEMS Taiwan" or "ReLeaf".
Abstract sheet, Goals: "it can prevent further deterioration" does not say what "it" is or what is harmed. Write "could stop further harm to soil and nearby ecosystems".
Abstract sheet: "all of which are targets" repeats the body slip. Write "goals".

notes.anchor: We have an education website where we compiled all of the education resources
notes.title: A good message to make bold
notes.body: This is something real that others can use after the season, and you put it in bold. Judges ask whether other teams can build on your work, and this answers it on the first screen. Add the link.
notes.excerpt_note: Queens says exactly what it hands over and how others reuse it.
notes.ballot: Has the team documented their work against their chosen SDG(s) so that other teams can build upon their work?

notes.title: Use your survey number here
notes.body: This line says what is on the website, not what changed for learners. You have a measured result for SDG 4, and it is the strongest number on the page. Put it here.
notes.after: biotic vs abiotic stress answers rose from 16% to 91% after our lessons
notes.excerpt_note: Heidelberg opens each section with a one-line result that has a number.
notes.ballot: Has the team's work measurably and significantly addressed one or more SDGs?

notes.title: This line works on its own
notes.body: Four words give the action and who it helps. A judge sees your SDG 10 plan without opening the section.

notes.anchor: Sustainability is not only limited to environmental sustainability, but also the sustainability of our societal structure
notes.title: Your own definition sets up the goals
notes.body: You say what sustainability means to your team, and you include people as well as the environment. This explains early why education (SDG 4) and inequality (SDG 10) belong on a page about farm technology. Keep the idea, and split the long sentence after it into two.

notes.anchor: we chose our SDGs first based on their relation to our project, then we narrowed it down based on which ones we can actually make an impact on
notes.title: A clear two-step choice
notes.body: You explain how you picked your goals: first by their link to the project, then by where you can really make a difference. Most winning pages just list their goals, so judges rarely see this reasoning. Keep this order.
notes.excerpt_note: UZurich also explains how it studied the problem before it lists any goal.

notes.anchor: while Climate Action can be affected through improving the environment through using our bioreactor, it isn’t the main point of our project
notes.title: Honest about a goal you dropped
notes.body: You admit your project might touch Climate Action, then explain why you do not claim it. This tells judges you will not overclaim, so your other four goals become more believable. Aalto-Helsinki, a 2025 winner, wins trust the same way by saying what its page will not claim.
notes.excerpt_note: See how Aalto states its project stage and limits before any goal.

notes.anchor: This is especially acute for farming families that not only sell their crops, but rely on their farm to feed themselves
notes.title: A real group with a real trade-off
notes.body: You name who is hurt most, families who eat what they grow, and the hard choice they face between eating and earning. This turns a world problem into people a judge can picture. It also links SDG 2 to the small farmers you write about under SDG 10.

notes.anchor: teachers can sign up for us to teach lessons for their classes inside that website
notes.title: A resource others can really use
notes.body: You point to something that lasts after the season: a website with your lessons where teachers can book a class. This is what judges mean by work others can build on. Add the link and say what is on it, such as lesson plans for three school levels.
notes.excerpt_note: Queens lists exactly what it hands over and how another team can reuse it.
notes.ballot: Has the team documented their work against their chosen SDG(s) so that other teams can build upon their work?

notes.anchor: or reservations regarding using newer products on their farmland, because of limited space
notes.title: Explain why small farms hold back
notes.body: "Because of limited space" does not explain why small farmers avoid new products. Say the reason in plain words. Add the Taiwan figure from your Geospatial Analysis page, which shows most farms are under 2 hectares.
notes.after: Most farms in Taiwan are small, under 2 hectares (see Geospatial Analysis). Small farmers told us [their reason], so they are careful with new technology.

notes.anchor: We plan to use the profit we obtain from selling devices to industrial farmers or selling data to researchers
notes.title: A concrete plan to share the cost
notes.body: You name who pays (industrial farms and researchers), who benefits (small farmers) and how (subsidies, or rentals through unions). This matches your Entrepreneurship page, where the idea of selling data came from a stakeholder. A mechanism like this is easy for a judge to check.

notes.anchor: This way, both sides of the spectrum can use and enjoy the benefits
notes.title: Add the SDG 10 work you already did
notes.body: Under SDG 10 you only describe a future plan. Your Human Practices page shows work already done for small farmers: the 農友助手 LINE account, built because many smallholders find it hard to get help online. Add it here, with a number if you have one.
notes.after: We have also built 農友助手, a LINE account that gives small farmers heat stress alerts and crop advice in an app they already use. [Number] farmers have joined so far.
notes.ballot: Has the team's work measurably and significantly addressed one or more SDGs?

notes.anchor: the safety measures in the bioreactor itself ensure containment unless under extenuating circumstances
notes.title: Name the safety layers and the risks
notes.body: "Safety measures" and "extenuating circumstances" are too vague to check. Entrepreneurship names three containment layers. Human Practices records Mr. Chen of the Lanyang River cooperative warning that disasters or wild animals could damage a reactor. Use both here.
notes.after: The bioreactor is designed to keep the engineered B. subtilis inside with three layers: a genetic kill switch, a hollow-fibre membrane and a sealed housing. Mr. Chen of the Lanyang River cooperative warned that typhoons or animals could break a reactor in the field, so we added this risk to the threat analysis in our business plan.
notes.excerpt_note: UZurich treats its own bacteria as an SDG 15 risk and lists each control measure.

notes.anchor: Here, we want to acknowledge those negatives as a part of our product that we hope we can change
notes.title: Add how you affect other SDGs
notes.body: Judges ask how your work affects other SDGs, and this section covers one risk only. For each one, name who loses, how, and which goal is hurt. Your other pages give you a start: power for the reactor (SDG 7), farm work (SDG 8), and older farmers (Human Practices says your buyers are mostly young farmers).
notes.after: SDG 7: The bioreactor needs steady power, so farms with [unreliable power] could [problem]. SDG 10: Most interest comes from young farmers, so older farmers could be left behind unless we [plan].
notes.excerpt_note: Both name who loses, how, and what the team does about it.
notes.ballot: How well has the team considered the positive and/or negative interactions of their work in relation to other SDGs?

notes.anchor: Due to the fact that our product always immediately supplies plants with the necessary protectants
notes.title: A real risk from your own product
notes.body: You name a specific way your product could do harm: plants may come to depend on it and lose their own resilience. It comes from a named farmer, and you do not hide it. Some winners fold their risks out of sight, so this paragraph is a strength.
notes.excerpt_note: Heidelberg also takes its own selling point and says where it could fail.
notes.ballot: How well has the team considered the positive and/or negative interactions of their work in relation to other SDGs?

notes.anchor: Plants that use our protectants will have a bit of a hard time building resilience on their own
notes.title: Close the loop on Ms. Chen
notes.body: The paragraph states the risk twice and then stops. Human Practices says her concern changed your plan for how much protectant is released. End with that change, then say what you have not tested yet.
notes.after: Because of her concern, we plan to release only as much protectant as the crop needs, so it can still build its own resilience. We have not yet tested whether protected plants become dependent. That would need [experiment].
notes.excerpt_note: Feedback first, then the change it caused, in two or three sentences.
notes.ballot: Did the team incorporate feedback from relevant Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) stakeholders into their work?

notes.anchor: From our geospatial analysis, it can be seen where our project will have the largest impacts
notes.title: Say where the impact is largest
notes.body: This sentence tells the reader an answer exists but does not give it. Your Geospatial Analysis page names the place, so say it in one line and link the page.
notes.after: Our Geospatial Analysis shows that small farms cluster on the western plain and in the south, where climate volatility is also higher. That is where ReLeaf could help most.
notes.ballot: Did the team address potential long-term social, environmental and economic impacts of their work (in the context of the SDG(s) they have chosen)?
